source_refs.note: Unnumbered heading 1. Levels of Access Control under Encapsulation, with Figure 3.2 and the BankAccount example (PDF 39-40, printed 35-36).

blocks.text: In Python, you can control the visibility of class members using specific naming prefixes:

items: Public Members: These are accessible from anywhere—inside or outside the class. By default, all members in Python are public (as shown in Figure 3.2). Syntax: self.attribute_name

Protected Members: These are intended for internal use within the class and its subclasses. It is a convention (not a restriction) to signal to other developers that the member should not be accessed from outside. Syntax: self._attribute_name (single underscore)

Private Members: These are highly restricted and cannot be easily accessed from outside the class. Python uses a mechanism called Name Mangling to change the internal name of the variable to prevent accidental access. Syntax: self.__attribute_name (double underscore)

blocks.alt: Encapsulation diagram: a User / Outside Class box. A green arrow with a tick, labelled Access allowed, goes to the Public Methods / Interface box (getValue(), setValue()) inside a Class Object box; a dotted arrow leads from the methods to the Private Data box (__private_variable). A red dashed line with a cross, labelled Direct access restricted, runs from the user to the private data.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2: Encapsulation diagram showing private and public variables (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 3.2 labels the private data _private_variable with one underscore, which in Python marks a protected member; a private member has two underscores, __private_variable, as drawn above.
